units.text: The Louisiana Purchase treaty signed on April 30, 1803, in Paris, France, was priced at $15 million, not $10 million.

judgement.reason: The passages state the treaty was signed on April 30, 1803, in Paris and priced at $15 million, which directly supports the claim, including that it was not $10 million.

units.text: The $15 million price included $11,250,000 for the territory and $3,750,000 to settle American claims against France.

judgement.reason: The passages state the total was $15 million and a note itemizes two conventions: $11,250,000 for payment and $3,750,000 for American claims, which together equal the total price.

units.text: The $10 million figure represented the amount the United States was initially prepared to pay for New Orleans only, not the entire Louisiana Territory.

judgement.reason: The passages discuss $15 million and 100 million francs prices but never mention a $10 million figure or that it was for New Orleans only.

units.text: Historical records from the National Archives confirm the final price was $15 million as specified in the treaty and accompanying conventions.

judgement.reason: The National Archives passages state the purchase price was $15 million and note the treaty and two conventions amount to $11,250,000 plus $3,750,000, totaling $15 million.

units.text: Wikipedia corroborates that the agreed price was $15 million, with financial details settled with the help of European bankers.

judgement.reason: The passages state the price was settled at 80 million francs ($15 million) and that European bankers Alexander Baring and Pierre Labouchère assisted in the financial negotiations, supporting both parts of the statement.

units.text: The claim that the Louisiana Purchase was priced at $10 million is contradicted by authoritative sources specifying the $15 million total.

judgement.reason: The passages repeatedly state the Louisiana Purchase price and total as $15 million, which directly contradicts a claim of $10 million.
